title: Binary Logistic Regression Assignment
text:
In this assignment, I will apply binary logistic regression analysis to investigate the factors associated with surviving the Titanic crash using titanic::titanic_train.
My objectives are to:

Specify and estimate several plausible competing binary logistic regression models using glmmTMB.
Compare nested models using likelihood-ratio tests (χ²).
Evaluate overall model fit using AIC and BIC.
Examine model diagnostics and assess assumptions relevant to binary logistic regression.
Select and interpret a preferred model, including transforming log-odds coefficients into odds ratios.
Report results reproducibly using tables, figures, and Quarto.

title: Binary Logistic Regression Assignment
section: 1. Load packages and prepare the data
text:
1. Load packages and prepare the data


Code
library(glmmTMB)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(broom.mixed)
library(performance)
library(gt)
library(readr)
library(DHARMa)
library(ggeffects)
library(titanic)

titanic <- titanic_train

# Keep the same complete-case sample for every model
titanic <- titanic |>
  select(Survived, Sex, Age, Pclass) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    Sex.Binary = case_when(
      Sex == "male" ~ 0,
      Sex == "female" ~ 1)) |>
  mutate(
    Survived.Char = case_when(
      Survived == 0 ~ "Died",
      Survived == 1 ~ "Survived")) |>
  mutate(
    Pclass.Char = case_when(
      Pclass == "1" ~ "First Class",
      Pclass == "2" ~ "Second Class",
      Pclass == "3" ~ "Third Class")) |>
  mutate(Pclass = factor(Pclass, levels = c(1, 2, 3))) |>
  select(Survived, Survived.Char, Sex, Sex.Binary, Pclass, Pclass.Char, Age)
 
n <- nrow(titanic)


This dataset contains complete-case data on 714 passengers. The binary outcome variable is Survived: whether the passenger survived (1) or died (0) in the Titanic crash. Several other variables summarize characteristics of the Titanic passengers that could influence survival.
For this lab assignment, I will focus on four variables:

Summary of exploratory patterns

title: Binary Logistic Regression Assignment
text:
3. Specify and estimate competing models

3.1. Research question and substantive predictions
Research Question: How are passenger Sex, Pclass, and Age associated with whether a passenger Survived the sinking of the Titanic?
Based on historical context from 1912 and maritime evacuation norms, I expect all three predictors to be meaningfully associated with survival:

Sex: Under the “women and children first” maritime evacuation protocol enforced during the 1912 disaster, female passengers were given priority access to lifeboats. Therefore, I predict that male passengers had substantially lower odds of surviving than female passengers.
Pclass: Ticket class serves as a proxy for SES. First Class passengers had cabins located on upper decks closer to the lifeboats and received preferential treatment during evacuation, whereas Third Class passengers were quartered on lower decks further from the boat deck. I predict that Second and Third Class passengers had lower odds of survival relative to First Class passengers.
Age: Because young children were prioritized alongside women when loading lifeboats and older passengers may have faced greater physical barriers reaching the upper decks in freezing conditions, I predict that older age is associated with lower odds of surviving, holding sex and ticket class constant.

These are predictions about statistical associations in observational data, not experimental causal effects.


3.2. Specify four nested models
I will fit an intercept-only baseline model and three increasingly complex substantive models:








Model
Formula
Purpose / Research rationale




mod0: Null
Survived ~ 1
Establish a baseline


mod1: Sex
Survived ~ Sex
Evaluate the association of sex with survival


mod2: Sex + Pclass
Survived ~ Sex + Pclass
Evaluate the additional contribution of ticket class


mod3: Sex + Pclass + Age
Survived ~ Sex + Pclass + Age
Evaluate the additional contribution of passenger age



The models are nested: each successive model contains all predictors from the preceding model, plus one additional predictor.


Code
mod0 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ 1,
  data = titanic,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

mod1 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex,
  data = titanic,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

mod2 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex + Pclass,
  data = titanic,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

mod3 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex + Pclass + Age,
  data = titanic,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)


summary(mod0)
summary(mod1)
summary(mod2)
summary(mod3)

confint(mod3)


3.3. How the interpretation of the intercept changes across models
In binary logistic regression, the intercept represents the predicted log-odds of the outcome (Survived = 1) when all predictors in the model equal zero or are at their reference levels. As predictors are added across my models, the reference group defined by the intercept becomes increasingly specific:

In mod1 (Survived ~ Sex), "female" is the reference category for Sex. The intercept (1.124) represents the estimated log-odds of survival for female passengers across all ticket classes and ages.
In mod2 (Survived ~ Sex + Pclass), Pclass = 1 (First Class) is the reference category for ticket class. The intercept increases to 2.334 and now represents the estimated log-odds of survival specifically for female passengers in First Class.
In mod3 (Survived ~ Sex + Pclass + Age), the continuous predictor Age is added. The intercept increases further to 3.777 and now represents the estimated log-odds of survival for a female passenger in First Class whose age is 0 years (a newborn female infant).

title: Binary Logistic Regression Assignment
text:
4. Compare model performance
I will evaluate the four competing models using three main performance metrics:

AIC (Akaike Information Criterion): Evaluates model fit while penalizing model complexity. Lower values indicate a preferred balance between fit and complexity.
BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion): Similar to AIC, but applies a stronger penalty for model complexity. Lower values are preferred.
Likelihood-ratio test (χ²): Tests whether adding predictors significantly improves model fit relative to the preceding nested model. A statistically significant p-value (p < .05) indicates that the additional predictors significantly improve model fit.


4.1. Compare models
Because my four models are nested and estimated on the exact same complete-case sample (n = 714), I can compare all four models in a single anova() call.


Code
tests <- anova(mod0, mod1, mod2, mod3)

The glance() function from the broom.mixed package returns a one-row data frame containing model-level statistics for each fitted model.

glance2 <- broom.mixed::glance(mod2)
glance3 <- broom.mixed::glance(mod3)

  glance2,

4.4. Interpret the model comparisons
Considering both model fit and complexity, mod3 (Survived ~ Sex + Pclass + Age) provides the best fit to the Titanic survival data. As predictors are added sequentially from mod0 to mod3, both AIC and BIC decrease substantially at every step: AIC drops from 966.52 (mod0) to 754.7 (mod1), 680.43 (mod2), and finally 657.28 (mod3), while BIC similarly drops from 971.09 (mod0) to 763.84 (mod1), 698.71 (mod2), and 680.14 (mod3). Furthermore, the nested likelihood-ratio tests indicate that every predictor addition produces a statistically significant improvement in model fit: adding Sex to the null model significantly improves fit (χ²(1) = 213.82, p < .001), adding Pclass significantly improves fit beyond Sex (χ²(2) = 78.27, p < .001), and adding Age significantly improves fit beyond Sex and Pclass (χ²(1) = 25.15, p < .001). Here, AIC, BIC, and the likelihood-ratio tests all support the exact same conclusion because the explanatory contribution of each added variable is large enough to easily overcome both the standard complexity penalty of AIC and the stricter sample-size penalty of BIC. Overall, this pattern demonstrates that while passenger sex accounts for the single largest reduction in deviance, Pclass and Age each explain unique, meaningful variation in survival outcomes.


Additional performance comparison

title: Binary Logistic Regression Assignment
text:
5. Evaluate binary logistic regression diagnostics
Based on the model comparisons in Section 4, I provisionally select the best-performing model (mod3: Sex + Pclass + Age) and evaluate whether it satisfies the diagnostic assumptions of binary logistic regression.


Code
selected_row <- comparison_table |>
  filter(Nested.p.value < .05) |>
  slice_tail(n = 1)

# Creating an object with my selected model's name for dynamic reporting
selected_name <- selected_row$Model

# Case matching for dynamic reporting
selected_model <- switch(
  selected_name,
  "mod0: Null" = mod0,
  "mod1: Sex" = mod1,
  "mod2: Sex + Pclass" = mod2,
  "mod3: Sex + Pclass + Age" = mod3
)


The provisionally selected model is mod3: Sex + Pclass + Age, with AIC = 657.283 and BIC = 680.138.
I now examine five key diagnostic criteria for mod3:

Linearity on the log-odds scale
No catastrophic collinearity
No complete separation
No influential outliers
Events per predictor


5.1. Linearity on the logit scale (DHARMa)


Code
set.seed(9041)
res_mod3 <- simulateResiduals(selected_model, n = 500, plot = FALSE)



The default DHARMa diagnostic plot


Code
plot(res_mod3)












5.2. Collinearity


Code
check_collinearity(selected_model)


# Check for Multicollinearity

vif_plot











5.3. Complete separation
I check for symptoms of complete or quasi-complete separation, which include:

Unusually large coefficient estimates or standard errors (e.g., SE > 5)
glmmTMB convergence warnings
Fitted probabilities of exactly 0 or 1 for specific predictor combinations

Inspecting mod3 reveals small, stable standard errors (all SEs < 0.40) and no convergence warnings, confirming that complete separation is not present.


5.4. Influential observations and outliers
Because traditional Cook’s distance is not directly implemented for glmmTMB, I use DHARMa::testOutliers() to test for overly influential observations or simulation outliers:


Code
testOutliers(res_mod3)

5.5. Events per predictor
A standard working guideline for binary logistic regression is to have at least 10 events (and 10 non-events) per estimated coefficient.


Code
n_event <- sum(titanic$Survived == 1)
n_nonevent <- sum(titanic$Survived == 0)
n_coef <- length(fixef(selected_model)$cond)
epv <- round(min(n_event, n_nonevent) / n_coef, 1)


In this dataset, there are 290 survivors (events) and 424 non-survivors (non-events) across 5 model coefficients (including the intercept and two dummy variables for Pclass), yielding 58 events per parameter—far exceeding the minimum threshold of 10.


5.6. Summary of diagnostic findings
Overall, the diagnostic checks indicate that the assumptions of binary logistic regression are well satisfied for mod3. First, collinearity is negligible: Variance Inflation Factors (VIFs) for Sex, Pclass, and Age are all near 1.0 (well below the conservative threshold of 5), indicating that each predictor contributes independent information and standard errors are not inflated. Second, there is no evidence of complete separation (all coefficients and standard errors are finite and small) and the sample size provides 58 events per parameter, ensuring stable maximum-likelihood estimation. Third, DHARMa::testOutliers() identifies no statistically significant outlier problem (p > .05), and the Q–Q plot of simulated scaled residuals closely tracks the uniform expectation line (non-significant Kolmogorov–Smirnov dispersion and uniformity tests). While the right-hand DHARMa residual-versus-predicted quantile plot shows minor local deviations across predicted probability quantiles—likely reflecting slight non-linearities or unmodeled interactions between sex and ticket class (for example, survival was particularly high for women in First and Second Class compared to Third Class)—these minor deviations do not compromise overall distributional uniformity or parameter stability. Consequently, I can retain and interpret mod3 with high confidence.

title: Binary Logistic Regression Assignment
section: 6. Select and report your preferred model
text:
6. Select and report your preferred model

6.1. Justification for preferred model (mod3)
Based on statistical fit, information criteria, diagnostics, and substantive theory, mod3 (Survived ~ Sex + Pclass + Age) is selected as the preferred model. Statistically, adding Age to Sex and Pclass yielded a highly significant likelihood-ratio test (χ²(1) = 25.15, p < .001) and achieved the lowest AIC (657.28) and lowest BIC (680.14) among all four candidate models. Although mod3 is the most complex specification tested, estimating five parameters with n = 714 observations remains parsimonious (58 events per parameter) and introduced zero collinearity or separation issues. Substantively, retaining all three predictors is essential because historical evacuation practices on the Titanic simultaneously depended on gender, age, and SES tied to passenger ticket class.


6.2. Extract binary logistic regression coefficients
I use broom.mixed::tidy() to extract the unstandardized log-odds coefficients and 95% confidence intervals from selected_model (mod3), and compute the corresponding odds ratios (or) and 95% odds-ratio confidence intervals (or.conf.low, or.conf.high) for dynamic inline reporting.


Code
coefficient_results <- broom.mixed::tidy(
  selected_model,
  effects = "fixed",
  component = "cond",
  conf.int = TRUE,
  conf.level = 0.95
) |>
  mutate(
    or = exp(estimate),
    or.conf.low = exp(conf.low),
    or.conf.high = exp(conf.high)
  )

7.2. Interpreting each predictor on the log-odds and odds-ratio scales
Every predictor in mod3 is interpreted while holding the remaining predictors in the model constant:

Sex (male vs. reference group female): Holding ticket class (Pclass) and Age constant, being male is associated with a decrease in the log-odds of surviving the Titanic crash of 2.52 (b = -2.52, SE = 0.21, p < .001). On the odds-ratio scale, holding ticket class and age constant, male passengers had 0.08 times the odds of surviving compared to female passengers (95% CI [0.05, 0.12]), meaning men’s odds of survival were approximately 92% lower than women’s.
Second Class (Pclass2 vs. reference group Pclass1 [First Class]): Holding passenger Sex and Age constant, traveling in Second Class rather than First Class is associated with a decrease in the log-odds of survival of 1.31 (b = -1.31, SE = 0.28, p < .001). Transformed into an odds ratio, holding sex and age constant, Second Class passengers had 0.27 times the odds of surviving compared to First Class passengers (95% CI [0.16, 0.47]), representing a 73% reduction in survival odds.
Third Class (Pclass3 vs. reference group Pclass1 [First Class]): Holding passenger Sex and Age constant, traveling in Third Class rather than First Class is associated with a decrease in the log-odds of survival of 2.58 (b = -2.58, SE = 0.28, p < .001). On the odds-ratio scale, holding sex and age constant, Third Class passengers had 0.08 times the odds of surviving compared to First Class passengers (95% CI [0.04, 0.13]), corresponding to a 92.4% reduction in the odds of survival.
Age (Age): Holding passenger Sex and ticket class (Pclass) constant, each one-year increase in age is associated with a decrease in the log-odds of survival of 0.04 (b = -0.04, SE = 0.01, p < .001). As an odds ratio, holding sex and ticket class constant, a one-year increase in age is associated with 0.96 times the odds of surviving (95% CI [0.95, 0.98]), or a 3.6% decrease in the odds of survival per additional year of age.



7.3. Overarching summary paragraph of results
To investigate the demographic and socioeconomic factors associated with surviving the sinking of the Titanic (n = 714), I estimated and compared a series of four nested binary logistic regression models using glmmTMB. Model comparisons using likelihood-ratio tests, AIC, and BIC consistently supported the full three-predictor model (mod3: Survived ~ Sex + Pclass + Age), which significantly improved model fit over simpler specifications (Δχ²(1) = 25.15, p < .001; AIC = 657.28, BIC = 680.14). In the preferred model, all three predictors were statistically significant and in the predicted directions. Controlling for ticket class and age, male passengers had substantially lower odds of surviving than female passengers, OR = 0.08, 95% CI [0.05, 0.12], p < .001. Socioeconomic status (measured via ticket class) was also strongly associated with survival: holding sex and age constant, passengers in Second Class (OR = 0.27, 95% CI [0.16, 0.47], p < .001) and Third Class (OR = 0.08, 95% CI [0.04, 0.13], p < .001) had markedly lower odds of surviving compared to First Class passengers. Finally, holding sex and ticket class constant, older age was associated with lower odds of surviving, OR = 0.96 per year, 95% CI [0.95, 0.98], p < .001.

8. Discuss findings and limitations

Substantive conclusions on relative predictor importance
The results of this analysis provide clear evidence that survival during the sinking of the Titanic was structured by a hierarchy of gender norms, socioeconomic status, and age:

Passenger Sex (Sex): Sex was the single strongest predictor of survival, accounting for the largest reduction in model deviance (Δχ² = 213.82). Holding ticket class and age constant, men had only 0.08 times the odds of surviving compared to women, reflecting strict adherence to the “women and children first” evacuation protocol.
Ticket Class (Pclass): Socioeconomic status was the second most influential factor (Δχ² = 78.27). Even when comparing passengers of the same sex and age, Second Class passengers had 73% lower odds of survival and Third Class passengers had 92.4% lower odds of survival than First Class passengers. Physical proximity to the boat deck and social privilege gave wealthy passengers a decisive survival advantage.
Age (Age): Age provided a smaller but still statistically significant incremental contribution (Δχ² = 25.15). Each additional year of age reduced the odds of survival by 3.6% holding sex and class constant, consistent with children receiving priority access to lifeboats and older adults facing greater physical challenges during the evacuation.



Limitations
Several methodological and substantive limitations should be kept in mind when interpreting my findings:

Missing data and complete-case restriction: Filtering the titanic_train dataset via drop_na() excluded 177 passengers who were missing Age records (reducing the sample from 891 to 714 passengers). Because Third Class passengers were disproportionately more likely to have unrecorded ages, complete-case analysis may introduce selection bias if missingness was not completely at random.
Additive main-effects specification: My preferred model (mod3) assumes additive effects on the logit scale (Survived ~ Sex + Pclass + Age). Historical records suggest that the benefit of being female was substantially weaker in Third Class than in First or Second Class; future analyses could test a Sex * Pclass interaction term to capture this moderation effect.
Unmeasured confounders: Other important passenger characteristics such as cabin location, number of siblings/spouses (SibSp) or parents/children (Parch) aboard, and language barriers were not included in my models and may partially confound the observed associations of ticket class and age with survival.
